speaker: haroldkleyw
text: Excellent. Okay, I'll try to watch the clock here and get through this in 10 minutes. So, we designed the replacement for the culvert and this is just a quick overview to give you a little bit of confidence in the design and the design approach. So, this culvert was added to the OSIM list of structures in 2018 when Keystone was involved in the inspection back when Steve Keeley was your Public Works Director. Steve was a classmate of mine, by the way, back in high school. The culverts are about 30 years old at this time. They are not a very good design in terms of passing water and one of the chief problems is that they are prone to obstructing because of their small diameter and the width of the stream. And the road platform over the culverts is on the narrow side. The drainage basin that is drained by these four culverts is shown in this slide here. It's almost 40 square kilometers in size. About 41% of the drainage basin is swamps and ponds. 29% is agriculture and about a quarter is forest. This culvert is designed for a flow that can be expected about once every 10 years. This is known as the Q10, so the one in 10 year flood and that amounts to 11 cubic meters per second. There's a check flood that is designed for as well, which is a hundred year return period and that's estimated to be 18 cubic meters per second. And as I noted, the existing culvert, the openings are constricted. There is some scour downstream, which means the water is flowing very quickly through the pipes and it's eroding the stream bed downstream and we found from our hydro technical analysis that in an extreme event, there's a good possibility that the road could overflow and you could lose the culverts. This is from some computer software we use to model the impact of, in this case, the check flood, the extreme flood. And what we found in the modeling is that the water could be backed up by over a meter high between the upstream and downstream side of the road. With that, there's a risk of the embankment, piping failure in the embankment, which is just like a quicksand type failure. And also the water level upstream is to the point that it's almost overtopped in the road. And depending on how well the stream is modeled, how accurately we've gauged the actual flows, the road could well overtop in a hundred year flood. We looked at two options for replacement. We looked at a corrugated steel pipe arch type culvert, which would have a span of 2.6 meters and a height of 1.8 meters. And we also looked at twin 2.4 by one and a half concrete box culverts. You know, for some of you, maybe feet are better. So an eight foot span by five foot height concrete box culvert is what we looked at. I certainly like feet a lot still. So when we modeled how the pipe arch culvert would operate compared to the concrete box culvert, we learned that the pipe arch culvert was not really any kind of an improvement over what's there presently. It would have to be a much larger pipe arch culvert to be an improvement. And that would mean raising the height of the road and it would add to the expense and to slightly to the complexity of the project. A concrete box culvert, because of it's just a better opening size and a smoother opening, it performs a whole lot better. And so what we learned was if we were to put in a concrete box culvert, the water levels under the design flood, the 10 year return period flood would be about 14 centimeters or six inches lower compared to what's existing. And under the extreme flood, water levels would be over a foot lower. And so the concrete box culvert is clearly an improvement over what's existing. And is a better choice compared to a pipe arch culvert. I don't really speak to it, but a corrugated steel pipe arch culvert will last about 35 to 40 years, whereas a concrete box culvert should last easily up to a hundred years. So here we are comparing, it's not quite an apples to apples comparison, but it shows how the concrete box culvert would operate under the design storm of about 11 cubic meters per second. And that's compared to the existing under the extreme flood. In any case, what's important to observe is that under the design flood, there's about a foot of clearance from the water level to the underside of the culvert. And that's desirable for design purposes. And it could point out that the water level under the extreme flood would be about a foot below the top of the road, or a foot below the top of Richardson Road. We did a survey in the field, and this is just a quick glimpse of a 3D model of what our survey looks like. And it shows the extent of the survey. We're proposing to close the road to install the culvert. And so the detour is somewhat lengthy. That takes us through Merrickville to get around the culvert site. Fortunately, as you probably know, there's not a lot of traffic on Richardson Road. And so the public won't be inconvenienced very much. The design looks like this in plan and sort of in cross section. We're showing you in cross section that six pieces, two and a half meters long times two barrels will be quite sufficient and will result in an improved road cross section. And to shorten up the culvert, we're proposing to use some concrete gravity blocks. So instead of making the culvert longer, we just use these concrete gravity blocks to shorten up the culvert, keep everything nicely within the right of way. And these concrete gravity blocks actually improve the flow through the culvert. And so that's an important consideration in the hydraulic design. Now we're showing a little bit of riprap around the inlet and the outlet of the culvert. And we're also showing guide rail. And the guide rail, we'll talk in a little bit more detail in a minute. It's a fairly expensive contribution to the overall cost. And we're showing it as provisional so that if we find that the project is a little bit over budget or we're trying to save some money for the township, then we could potentially consider not installing the guide rail at this time. A couple of more views, an end view of the culvert showing the riprap and what the end of the culvert looks like. It's showing about two feet of cover over top of the culvert, which is the minimum amount of gravel that needs to be placed over top of the culvert for the culverts to pass a full truckload. The new road cross section we're showing an eight meter cross section from face of guide rail to face of guide rail. That's a very generous cross section. And that will serve the township for a good long time at this location. So in terms of budget breakdown, the concrete culvert pieces and the gravity blocks are estimated to cost about 170,000. The granulars for the project around 24,000. The guide rail 43,000, which is a very significant component of the cost. And we show that as being provisional. And then for removals of the culvert excavation and dewatering, our estimates about 26,000. And other sundry costs about 48,000 for a total budget cost of $311,000. I normally, when asked to make these things, I'm conservative, meaning that in actuality, the price should come in well below 300,000, but for budgeting purposes. And so there's no sticker shock afterwards. The engineering estimate at this time is 311. And again, I point out that $43,000 could be taken away quite easily if an election was made not to install the guide rail at this time. I'm recommending that the township provides an incentive to the contractor. Without an incentive, the project should take about 10 days to complete. With an incentive, the road closure could be reduced to seven days or possibly less. And so in the contract language, I've provided for $1,000 a day incentive to open the road early. Now, of course, this can be reduced or increased depending on, or eliminated altogether, depending on how council views this particular suggestion. And this is a somewhat similar culvert, much larger culvert, but this just gives you an idea of approximately what the design solution we've recommended will look like. And that concludes my presentation.
